source.document: WHO SMART Guidelines — Antenatal Care (DAK L2)

regles.action: Conduct ultrasound at the health-care facility or the referral facility
regles.annotation: An ultrasound is recommended for all women before 24 weeks gestation
regles.reference: WHO ANC recommendations (2016): B.2.4. Ultrasound scan (3)

regles.action: Conduct ultrasound at the health-care facility or the referral facility optional if deemed necessary by the health worker
regles.annotation: An ultrasound is recommended for all women even after 24 weeks gestation if deemed necessary (e.g. to identify the number of fetuses, fetal presentation or placenta location)
regles.reference: WHO ANC recommendations (2016): B.2.4. Ultrasound scan (3)

regles.sortie: "Referral for screening including diagnostics and lab testing" = FALSE
regles.annotation: An ultrasound is recommended for all women before 24 weeks gestation or even after if deemed necessary (e.g. to identify the number of fetuses, fetal presentation or placenta location).  An early ultrasound is key to estimate gestational age, improve detection of fetal anomalies and multiple fetuses, reduce induction of labour for post-term pregnancy, and improve a woman’s pregnancy experience.
regles.reference: WHO ANC recommendations (2016): B.2.4. Ultrasound scan (3)

regles.sortie: "Referral for screening including diagnostics and lab testing" = TRUE
regles.action: Refer to a facility with ultrasound equipment
regles.annotation: If an ultrasound cannot be conducted at the health-care facility, the woman should be referred to another health-care facility in which she can receive an ultrasound.  An ultrasound is recommended for all women before 24 weeks gestation or even after if deemed necessary (e.g. to identify the number of fetuses, fetal presentation or placenta location).  An early U/S is key to estimate gestational age, improve detection of fetal anomalies and multiple fetuses, reduce induction of labour for post-term pregnancy, and improve a woman’s pregnancy experience.
regles.reference: WHO ANC recommendations (2016): B.2.4. Ultrasound scan (3)

regles.condition: "Population prevalence of HIV in pregnant women" ≥ 5%
regles.annotation: In high-prevalence settings, provider-initiated testing and counselling (PITC) for HIV should be considered a routine component of the package of care for pregnant women in all ANC settings  An HIV test is required for all pregnant women at the first contact in pregnancy if the HIV prevalence in the pregnant woman population is 5% or higher.
regles.reference: WHO ANC recommendations (2016): B.1.7. Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and syphilis (3)

regles.condition: "Population prevalence of HIV in pregnant women" ≥ 5%
regles.annotation: Another HIV test is required for all pregnant women at the first contact of the 3rd trimester (28 weeks), if the HIV prevalence in the pregnant woman population is 5% or higher
regles.reference: WHO ANC recommendations (2016): B.1.7. Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and syphilis (3)

regles.condition: "Population prevalence of HIV in pregnant women" < 5%
regles.annotation: In low-prevalence settings, provider-initiated testing and counselling (PITC) can be considered for pregnant women in ANC settings as a key component of the effort to eliminate mother-to-child transmission of HIV, and to integrate HIV testing with syphilis, viral or other key tests, as relevant to the setting, and to strengthen the underlying maternal and child health systems
regles.reference: WHO ANC recommendations (2016): B.1.7. Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and syphilis (3)

regles.annotation: A test is not required if the woman is already confirmed HIV positive
regles.reference: WHO ANC recommendations (2016): B.1.7. Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and syphilis (3)

regles.annotation: Hepatitis B testing is recommended for at-risk women. HBsAg laboratory-based immunoassay is the preferred method for testing for Hep B infection in pregnancy; if immunoassay is not available, HBsAg rapid diagnostic test (RDT) is recommended over dried blood spot (DBS) HBsAg testing.
regles.reference: Guidelines on hepatitis B and C testing (2017): Recommendation 2 (4)
Guidelines on hepatitis B and C testing (2017): Recommendation (4)

regles.reference: Guidelines on hepatitis B and C testing 92017): Recommendation 11 (4)

regles.condition: "Occupation" = "Employment that puts woman at increased risk for HIV (e.g. sex worker)"
regles.reference: Guidelines on hepatitis B and C testing (2017): Recommendation 14 (4)

regles.sortie: "Hepatitis C test required" = TRUE "Population prevalence of hepatitis C" ≥ 2%
regles.annotation: In settings where the proportion of HCV antibody seroprevalence in the general population is 2% or higher, then a hepatitis C test is required.  Anti-HCV laboratory-based immunoassay is the preferred method for testing for Hep C infection in pregnancy; if immunoassay is not available, anti-HCV rapid diagnostic test (RDT) is recommended over dried blood spot (DBS) anti-HCV testing.
regles.reference: Guidelines on hepatitis B and C testing (2017): Recommendation 6.1 (4)

regles.sortie: "Hepatitis C test required" = TRUE "HIV status" = "HIV positive"
regles.annotation: If the woman is HIV positive, then a hepatitis C test is required.  Anti-HCV laboratory-based immunoassay is the preferred method for testing for Hep C infection in pregnancy; if immunoassay is not available, anti-HCV rapid diagnostic test (RDT) is recommended over dried blood spot (DBS) anti-HCV testing
regles.reference: Guidelines on hepatitis B and C testing (2017): Recommendation 6.1 (4)

regles.condition: "Current alcohol and/or other substance use" = "Injectable drugs"
regles.sortie: "Hepatitis C test required" = TRUE "Current alcohol and/or other substance use" = "Injectable drugs"
regles.annotation: If the woman injects drugs, then a hepatitis C test is required.  Anti-HCV laboratory-based immunoassay is the preferred method for testing for Hep C infection in pregnancy; if immunoassay is not available, anti-HCV rapid diagnostic test (RDT) is recommended over dried blood spot (DBS) anti-HCV testing.
regles.reference: Guidelines on hepatitis B and C testing (2017): Recommendation 6.1 (4)

regles.sortie: "Hepatitis C test required" = TRUE "Occupation" = "Informal employment (sex worker)"
regles.annotation: If a woman is a sex worker, then a hepatitis C test is required.  Anti-HCV laboratory-based immunoassay is the preferred method for testing for Hep C infection in pregnancy; if immunoassay is not available, anti-HCV rapid diagnostic test (RDT) is recommended over dried blood spot (DBS) anti-HCV testing.
regles.reference: Guidelines on hepatitis B and C testing (2017): Recommendation 6.1 (4)

regles.annotation: A syphilis test is recommended for all pregnant women at the first contact
regles.reference: WHO ANC recommendations (2016): B.1.7. Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and syphilis (3)

regles.annotation: A syphilis test is recommended again at the first contact of 3rd trimester (28 weeks)
regles.reference: WHO ANC recommendations (2016): B.1.7. Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and syphilis (3)

regles.annotation: Women who are already confirmed positive for syphilis do not need to be tested
regles.reference: WHO ANC recommendations (2016): B.1.7. Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and syphilis (3)

regles.sortie: "Urine test required" = TRUE - Pain during urination
regles.annotation: Urine test is required any time the woman reports pain during urination (dysuria)
regles.reference: Managing complications guide (IMPAC) (2017): Section S-51 (3)

regles.action: Do urine dipstick test for protein
regles.annotation: Given high values (SBP ≥ 140 or DBP ≥ 90) upon second measure, urine dipstick test should be done to check for protein in the urine, a symptom of pre-eclampsia
regles.reference: Managing complications guide (IMPAC) (2017): Section S-51 (3)

regles.action: Do urine dipstick test for protein
regles.annotation: Given high values (SBP ≥ 140 or DBP ≥ 90) upon second measure, urine dipstick test should be done to check for protein in the urine, a symptom of pre-eclampsia
regles.reference: Managing complications guide (IMPAC) (2017): Section S-51 (3)

regles.annotation: The urine test checks for bacterial or other infections that can lead to adverse outcomes for the neonate. The urine dipstick test can check for proteins in the urine, which can be a sign of pre-eclampsia. Midstream urine culture is the preferred method for testing for asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB) in pregnancy; if culture is not available, midstream urine Gram-staining is recommended over dipstick.  Urine dipstick tests should only be used to diagnose ASB in pregnancy if midstream culture and Gram-staining are not possible. Dipstick tests are required to check for protein in the urine, a symptom of pre-eclampsia.
regles.reference: WHO ANC recommendations (2016): B.1.2. Asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB) (3)

regles.annotation: In settings where the tuberculosis (TB) prevalence in the general population is 100/100,000 persons or higher or in settings with sub-populations that have very poor access to health care, or if the woman is HIV positive, TB screening is recommended
regles.reference: WHO ANC recommendations (2016): B.1.8. Tuberculosis (TB) (3)
